    Sources indicate that right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI claims it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    It has been revealed that “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres noted. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Sources indicate that mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    In a recent development, to reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Sources indicate that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is presently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for significant investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    It has been revealed that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he stated. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler mentioned. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Industry observers note that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Recent findings suggest that today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler stated. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres remarked. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    It has been revealed that what video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler mentioned.).

    Recent findings suggest that “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler stated. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Recent findings suggest that part of the problem, he stated, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, wordPress unveiled the release of version 7.1.5, a security enhancement that fixes 18 vulnerabilities plus two security improvements. The update addresses several types of vulnerabilities, including cross-site scripting and SQL injection, as well as an unauthenticated flaw that could lead to remote code execution.

    WordPress 7.1.5 fixes 20 issues covering a range of vulnerabilities across WordPress core. One of the vulnerabilities in particular stands out because it could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover.

    It has been revealed that the first one that stands out is an unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerability affecting the Template Part block attributes which could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover. There is no authentication required to exploit this vulnerability, and it could lead to RCE. That combination is the worst-case scenario for a CMS.

    A remote code execution (RCE) is a vulnerability that enables an attacker to run their own code on someone else’s server from somewhere else, usually over the internet. For a WordPress site, that means the attacker can make the web server execute commands of their choosing. From there they can read or change files and make entries to the database, create admin accounts, install backdoors, or inject malware.

    Multisite Administrator to Super Admin takeover (Customizer menu previews). This vulnerability requires an Administrator account, but on a multisite installation that means that an attacker who achieves admin level credential on one site can attain control of the entire network of sites.

    In a recent development, unauthenticated stored XSS via shortcode attributes in comments. No login is needed to exploit it. Stored XSS is a type of flaw that can run malicious code in the browser of anyone who views the affected comment, including administrators, which can lead to account takeover.

    Two SQL injection vulnerabilities:.

    WordPress urges site owners to patch to version 7.1.5 immediately to address security vulnerabilities. The update is available through the WordPress dashboard or as a download, with automatic updates supported. Security fixes are also available for older affected WordPress versions, although only the latest version is actively supported.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one tech giant or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    In a recent development, collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Newly introduced Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently stated no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Latest Orleans Bowl.

    Industry observers note that I love Upcoming Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Newly introduced Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Newly introduced Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No.".

    According to recent reports, we asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    In a recent development, camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.     Sources indicate that hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    According to recent reports, we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    In a recent development, you will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling latest features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    Industry observers note that camunda is an AI-first organization, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    This is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for upcoming features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce issues, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product tech giant, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    It has been revealed that threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    Sources indicate that you read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    It has been revealed that you build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    Clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    According to recent reports, willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a major part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Upcoming York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    Recent findings suggest that in another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    According to recent reports, “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Industry observers note that hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I remarked there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

    Tameez: Tell me about why this work is key to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it.     Industry observers note that tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

    Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s.

    She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.”.

    That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that.

    In a recent development, but the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    In a recent development, redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

    Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    Sources indicate that redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Sources indicate that for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have remarked this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    It has been revealed that last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    Recent findings suggest that redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

    According to recent reports, redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

    Industry observers note that I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

    @MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

    Sources indicate that redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

    Industry observers note that creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile customers and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).
    • Recent findings suggest that for years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps.
    • Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that on Nov. 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile customers and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).

    Recent findings suggest that for years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps. When a person opened a sitemap URL in a browser, Chrome executed that XSLT file to transform the underlying XML code into a clean, clickable HTML table.

    Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that search engines do not use XSLT. Googlebot, Bingbot, and other web crawlers fetch and parse the raw XML nodes (, ) at the source. Crawlers avoid browser-side stylesheets, meaning indexing, crawl efficiency, and search rankings remain unaffected.

    Because Chrome 158 lands while Google’s November core update, which began on Nov. 10, is still rolling, site owners and clients checking their domains during routine ranking audits may panic when they see raw XML in place of the familiar formatted table.

    Depending on your site configuration, WordPress serves its sitemap index from one of two primary URLs:.

    If you open either URL in Chrome 158 or a newer release, seeing a wall of XML tags confirms the browser skipped the XSLT stylesheet, not that the sitemap file is corrupt or broken.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    To verify, or prove to a nervous client, that Google reads the sitemap without trouble, check Google Search Console:.

    As long as Search Console reports “Success,” Google parses the XML structure without error.

    Industry observers note that XML sitemaps exist for machine consumption, and search engine bots read the underlying and tags. Dropping visual styling changes nothing about URL discovery, crawl budget, or search visibility.

    Because Chrome 158 arrives alongside the November core update, clients or stakeholders who inspect their sitemap URLs will spot unformatted XML code and assume a site outage or plugin failure caused ranking fluctuations.

    Chrome logs a deprecation warning in DevTools whenever a page invokes an .xsl stylesheet. Automated site-health crawlers or QA tools that monitor browser console errors may flag sitemap URLs until plugins or WordPress core drop the stylesheet reference.

    Editors and junior marketers who relied on opening /sitemap_index.xml in Chrome as a quick directory of site URLs lose that visual table unless they switch browsers (such as Firefox or Safari, which retain XSLT for the time being) or use a dedicated HTML sitemap.

    Because search crawlers ignore XSLT, you don’t need to rush to make emergency fixes. Choose from the steps below based on your role and client needs:.

    It has been revealed that note: This is only a visual change. Chrome 158’s removal of XSLT support only affects how sitemaps render in human browsers. Search engine crawlers process raw XML directly and are completely unaffected.

    Organic performance, indexing, and rankings remain safe. WordPress 7.2 will remove the stylesheet reference and, with it, the Chrome warnings, leaving core sitemaps as plain XML. Yoast SEO 28.9 will restore a styled view using CSS, while Rank Math and AIOSEO have not announced a change.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the tech giant to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an revision to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    Industry observers note that meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting newly introduced commercial terms into effect.

    “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms enhancement. We care deeply about our partners and do not strategy to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    In a recent development, since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the manufacturer was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    According to recent reports, we're looking for a Developer Relations Engineer to join our team and help more developers discover, learn, and build with Supabase. You'll create high-impact content, build real-world projects, and represent Supabase across communities and events. If you're equally energized by writing code and teaching others, this is the role for you.

    Supabase is growing fast with 350,000+ developers, 1,000+ OSS contributors, and a thriving open source ecosystem. Our owners are builders, startup founders, weekend hackers, and engineers scaling to millions of users. DevRel is how we meet them where they are: through content, community, and code.

    We're building a community of communities that brings together developers from many backgrounds, including first-time open source contributors. As a DevRel Engineer, you'll be a bridge between Supabase and the broader developer ecosystem, helping people get started, go deep, and feel connected.

    Make content — Publish compelling technical content, especially video, to help developers learn Supabase promptly.

    Build demos and tutorials — Ship real-world apps using Supabase and tools like Next.js, React, and Stripe. Write guides that others can follow and remix.

    In a recent development, represent Supabase — Speak at meetups, livestream builds, and engage with the developer ecosystem. You'll be a visible and trusted voice of the platform.

    Support and grow the community — Celebrate contributors, answer questions, highlight cool projects, and bring developer feedback to the team.

    Collaborate across the firm — Work with engineering, product, and growth to amplify launches, prioritize content, and reduce friction for new users.

    You've built full-stack apps and enjoy sharing your knowledge.

    You create content that makes people want to open their code editor.

    You're equally comfortable writing a video script and TypeScript.

    You're energized by community whether it's on Discord, Twitter, YouTube, or in person.

    You're self-directed, organized, and excited to contribute to open source.

    Experience creating technical content (written or video).

    A growing audience on YouTube, Twitch, or Twitter.

    Prior experience in DevRel or open source.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    A fresh study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one significant takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    It has been revealed that that truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty latest. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a major gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Sources indicate that canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    Industry observers note that “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    Breaking: Attorney, New Verticals at Atticus

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve.
    • It has been revealed that so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve. In the last six years, we've become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We’re also rapidly scaling an injury practice to help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    It has been revealed that so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews. And we're just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, GV (Google Ventures), and True Ventures, with ambitions to create a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Each month, tens of thousands of Americans seek our help for a single legal matter – applying for Social Security Disability, filing a Workers’ Compensation claim – but many of these clients are actually eligible for additional aid without ever knowing it.

    Your job as Lead Attorney, Fresh Verticals is to help us do right by these clients, helping them claim additional benefits through the social safety net. You’ll oversee the team of intake specialists who speak with clients who have secondary claims, evaluating the case facts and whether to connect them with an Atticus attorney or local attorney to provide legal advice and potentially take on their case.

    This is a job that straddles the line between practicing the law and growing a business. It requires developing a strong understanding of multiple fields of law, and being able to accurately identify when we can help and when we cannot. But even more importantly, this job requires you to be an incredibly strong operator: you need to keep the big picture in mind and stay laser-focused on how we can achieve our goals, oftentimes finding outside-the-box ways to accomplish them. You will report to our General Manager of New Verticals and work closely with our CEO and Managing Attorney.

    On any given day, you’ll spend your time:.

    Speaking with severely injured clients trying to rebuild their lives after a catastrophic accident.

    Sourcing and vetting local counsel in individual markets, holding a high bar for representation quality and ending relationships that fall below it.

    Working with our data and insights team to identify existing clients who may have unrecognized claims in adjacent fields of law, and setting the standard for which ancillary cases we take on.

    Building the playbook for claim types we haven't handled before, starting by screening cases yourself and eventually creating the protocol our intake specialists will run at scale.

    This is a rare opportunity for an attorney to join a profitable and growing public-interest law firm and take on one of our biggest priorities as a company.

    You can understand the nuances of various contingency fields of law and can apply them to a variety of cases (including Social Security Disability, Workers’ Compensation, Personal Injury, and more) – you don’t need to be an expert today, but you should be a fast learner.

    You can empathize with anyone and rapidly build rapport and relationships while exercising good judgment, both with our clients and local counsel at law firms across the country.

    You have strong instincts and judgment as an operator – you can run effective and efficient processes, and you don’t let them run you.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You’ve built a track record as a great people manager – you know how to motivate talent and hold a high bar for output.

    You have meaningful work experience outside of serving as a lawyer, ideally at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment (e.g., a business operations team).

    It has been revealed that we are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you're from a background that's underrepresented in tech, we'd love to meet you.

    This role offers a unique chance to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our success.

    Sources indicate that we're a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    In a recent development, we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $140,000 and $175,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    It has been revealed that this job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the organization dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.
